title: Job 31:24–40
context: Job completes his oath of clearance. In 31:24–40 he disowns trust in wealth, secret worship of the sun and moon, gloating over an enemy, stinginess toward guests and travelers, and hiding his faults out of fear of public opinion. At 31:35–37 he breaks off into a climactic appeal: he signs his case and asks the Almighty to answer him, ready to wear the indictment like a crown. A final oath about his land follows (31:38–40), and the narrator closes, “The words of Job are ended.” Job does not speak again until he answers the LORD (40:3–5; 42:1–6). In 31:33, the WEB reads “like Adam”; some translations render the phrase “as men do” or “as others do.” The notes keep both senses in view and make no claim about manuscripts. Some readers notice that the land oath follows the climactic appeal; the notes read it where it stands.

verses.text: “If I have made gold my hope, and have said to the fine gold, ‘You are my confidence;’
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns making gold his hope or calling fine gold his confidence. Arminian readers note that Job was very wealthy (compare 1:3), yet claims he never let riches displace his trust in God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see trust in gold as a form of idolatry, misplaced confidence that belongs to God alone. Both traditions read the verse as Job’s denial that wealth ever became the foundation of his security.

verses.text: If I have rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because my hand had gotten much;
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns rejoicing because his wealth was great and his hand had gained much. Arminian readers see the difference between enjoying a gift and glorying in it as one’s own achievement, which Job denies doing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job attributes no merit to his prosperity and refuses pride in possessions. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a guard against the subtle pride that wealth can produce.

verses.text: if I have seen the sun when it shined, or the moon moving in splendor,
verses.arminianNotes: Job recalls seeing the sun shine and the moon moving in splendor. Arminian readers note that the heavenly bodies were widely worshiped in the ancient world, and that Job admired them without turning admiration into worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse alongside warnings against worshiping sun and moon, compare Deuteronomy 4:19 by reference. Both traditions read the line as setting up Job’s denial of secret idolatry.

verses.text: and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my hand threw a kiss from my mouth;
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns his heart being secretly enticed and his hand throwing a kiss from his mouth. Arminian readers see a gesture of private devotion to the heavenly lights, which Job insists he never offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the word secretly: Job denies even hidden, inward idolatry that no one else could see. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job claiming that his worship belonged wholly to God.

verses.text: this also would be an iniquity to be punished by the judges, for I would have denied the God who is above.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says such worship would be an iniquity punishable by the judges, for he would have denied the God above. Arminian readers note that Job sees idolatry as a real denial of God, a betrayal of the relationship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as recognizing that worshiping the creation instead of the Creator is the root sin of idolatry. Both traditions read Job’s words as affirming exclusive devotion to the one God above all.

verses.text: “If I have rejoiced at the destruction of him who hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns rejoicing at the ruin of someone who hated him or exulting when evil came upon him. Arminian readers see a striking ethic: Job claims to have refused even the inward satisfaction of an enemy’s downfall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the resonance with wisdom teaching against gloating, compare Proverbs 24:17 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a high standard of heart toward enemies, set out in the oath.

verses.text: (I have certainly not allowed my mouth to sin by asking his life with a curse);
verses.arminianNotes: In a parenthesis Job says he never let his mouth sin by asking his enemy’s life with a curse. Arminian readers note that Job extends his integrity to his speech, refusing words that call down harm on others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as restraint of the tongue, even toward someone who wronged him. Both traditions read the parenthesis as Job’s claim that his words matched the generous attitude of his heart.

verses.text: if the men of my tent have not said, ‘Who can find one who has not been filled with his meat?’
verses.arminianNotes: Job appeals to the men of his tent, asking who could find anyone not filled with his meat. Arminian readers see his household as witnesses to open-handed hospitality, offered freely to all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the testimony of those closest to Job carries weight, since they saw his daily conduct. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job citing others’ experience of his generosity, not merely his own claim.

verses.text: (the foreigner has not camped in the street, but I have opened my doors to the traveler);
verses.arminianNotes: Job says the foreigner did not camp in the street, for he opened his doors to the traveler. Arminian readers see hospitality to strangers as a central virtue in Job’s world, which he claims to have practiced fully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that welcoming the stranger is a recurring biblical duty, rooted in God’s own care for the sojourner. Both traditions read the verse as Job claiming that outsiders found shelter with him.

verses.text: if like Adam I have covered my transgressions, by hiding my iniquity in my heart,
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns covering his transgressions like Adam, hiding his iniquity in his heart. Arminian readers note that if Adam is meant, the line may recall Genesis 3:8–10 by reference; some translations read as men do instead, and the notes leave the choice open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise allow both renderings and note that either way Job denies concealing sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job claiming openness about his faults, not sinlessness, and neither builds doctrine on the wording.

verses.text: because I feared the great multitude, and the contempt of families terrified me, so that I kept silence, and didn’t go out of the door—
verses.arminianNotes: Job explains that he never hid his faults out of fear of the crowd or the contempt of families, keeping silent indoors. Arminian readers see social pressure as a real temptation Job claims he refused to let silence him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job ties concealment to fear of people rather than fear of God. Both traditions read the verse as Job’s claim that public opinion never drove him into hypocrisy or hiding, and the long sentence breaks off here.

verses.text: oh that I had one to hear me! Behold, here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me! Let the accuser write my indictment!
verses.arminianNotes: Job breaks off into his climactic appeal: he wishes for someone to hear him, signs his case, and asks the Almighty to answer and the accuser to write the charge. Arminian readers see Job’s bold request for a genuine hearing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job’s desire to argue his case before God runs through the book (compare 13:22; 23:3–7). Shared ground: both traditions read the appeal as honest protest within faith, which God will answer, though not as Job expects.

verses.text: Surely I would carry it on my shoulder, and I would bind it to me as a crown.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says he would carry the indictment on his shoulder and bind it to himself as a crown. Arminian readers see his confidence that any written charge, once examined, would prove his innocence and become an honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the boldness of the image and that the LORD’s later speeches will humble Job without accusing him of the crimes the friends alleged. Both traditions read the verse as Job’s certainty of his own integrity.

verses.text: I would declare to him the number of my steps. I would go near to him like a prince.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says he would declare to God the number of his steps and approach him like a prince. Arminian readers see Job’s willingness to give a full account of his life, holding nothing back from God’s scrutiny.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast with 31:4, where God counts Job’s steps; here Job offers to count them himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the princely posture as Job’s confidence, which the encounter in chapters 38–42 will reshape.

verses.text: If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep together;
verses.arminianNotes: Job returns to the oath form: if his land cries out against him and its furrows weep together. Arminian readers see the land personified as a witness, as though the soil itself could testify to injustice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the biblical motif of the ground bearing witness to wrongdoing, compare Genesis 4:10 by reference. Both traditions read the verse as Job’s claim that even his fields could not accuse him of injustice.

verses.text: if I have eaten its fruits without money, or have caused its owners to lose their life,
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns eating the land’s produce without payment or causing its owners to lose their lives. Arminian readers see a denial of exploiting laborers or seizing property, injustices that were common among the powerful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel with stories of land seized from its rightful owners, which Scripture treats as grave sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s claim to economic justice toward those who worked or owned land.

verses.text: let briers grow instead of wheat, and stinkweed instead of barley.” The words of Job are ended.
verses.arminianNotes: Job’s last self-curse asks for briers instead of wheat and stinkweed instead of barley, and then the narrator says Job’s words are ended. Arminian readers see Job resting his case, having laid his whole life open before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the closing line marks a pause: Job has spoken, and the next voices are Elihu’s and then the LORD’s. Both traditions read the end of the oath as Job’s final protest of integrity, left for God to answer.
